parts.name: Passage 1
parts.passageHtml:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1–13, which are based on Reading Passage 1 below.

The Blockbuster Phenomenon: A New Museum Trend

Museums in Australia, like other pleasure-giving public organizations, are adapting their activities so that they more closely reflect the marketplace.

A. Since the 1980s, the word blockbuster has become a fashionable term in the museum world. It refers to spectacular and high-profile exhibitions that attract large crowds. In 1984, Eisen defined a blockbuster as a large-scale loan exhibition. He said even people who rarely visit museums were willing to queue for one. The model was visible at the British Museum in London. The Treasures of Tutankhamun ran from 30 March to 30 December 1972. It was originally planned for six months. However, it was extended because of demand. The exhibition displayed 50 objects. It attracted 1,694,117 visitors — more than 7,000 a day. Once a successful exhibition reaches its local audience, it may be offered to other institutions for a fee. In this way, one museum can boost its takings. It can also earn income from another museum's audience.

B. Visitors lured by a major temporary exhibition may not leave after viewing its main objects. They may continue through the galleries, partaking in a broader museum experience. Betty Churcher was Director of the Australian National Gallery from 1990 to 1997. The gallery was later renamed the National Gallery of Australia. She argued that people arriving for a blockbuster often stayed to examine the permanent collection. This gave the museum's existing holdings greater exposure. A similar attraction occurred in New York in 2010. Picasso in The Metropolitan Museum of Art (the Met) drew 703,256 visitors in 17 weeks. The exhibition included 300 works from the Met's own collection.

C. Museums in the UK, USA, Canada and Australia frequently operate under a system of plural funding. Part of their revenue comes from government contributions at the federal, state or local level. The rest may come from admission charges, memberships, shops, restaurants or special exhibitions. Maintaining visitor levels is therefore paramount. Museums now make regular changes to their programmes. They also compete for major travelling shows. As a result, the public may be described as customers rather than visitors. Curators often take on administrative duties. Meanwhile, directors require public relations skills. These skills help their institutions compete successfully to stage exhibitions that attract large audiences.

D. The growing convergence of museums, tourism and commerce has produced what some call the new museology. This trend has caused debate. Some writers describe blockbusters as non-elitist and too commercial. Others extol the virtues of cooperation across museums. They say such projects can cater for a wide community rather than an elite one. The Museum of Modern Art in New York (MoMA) collaborated with Tate and museums in Paris on Matisse Picasso. The exhibition was shown at MoMA from 13 February to 19 May 2003. Whatever commentators say, museum managers continue to combine culture with commerce.

E. Blockbusters can bring an institution a surplus. However, their financial benefits vary. The British Museum states that profits from its 1972 Tutankhamun exhibition were donated to major cultural projects in Egypt. The Louvre provides a later example of remarkable public demand. Its Leonardo da Vinci exhibition was held from 24 October 2019 to 24 February 2020. It received 1,071,840 visitors in 104 days. This was higher than the 540,000 visitors recorded for its 2018 Delacroix retrospective. Such income can help museums fund new acquisitions. It can also pay for specific repairs, such as leaking roofs and faulty temperature controls. In Australia, a blockbuster may also illustrate that a museum is recovering part of its running costs. Its positive spin-offs may extend to hotels, restaurants, shops and public transport. This supports claims that the arts have sustained economic benefits.

F. The attraction of large attendance figures should not hide the costs. Blockbusters require major capital expenditure. This includes money for loans, insurance, shipping, security, installation and marketing. One published Australian estimate placed the cost of mounting a major imported blockbuster at A$3.5–4.5 million. There is also a cost in staff time. A touring exhibition draws resources from several functional departments. Staff in services, front-of-house, technical, promotional, educational and administrative roles may all have to perform additional tasks. As the Met, MoMA, the Louvre and Australian galleries compete for attention, the market becomes crowded. Successful shows may therefore be less likely to produce enough profit to subsidize other activities. This is because of the competitive nature of the market.

G. Experience in the UK and USA suggests that the blockbuster ideology can create a false expectation. Some museums believe that the momentum behind a successful programme can be sustained indefinitely. However, mounting major shows is tiring for staff. Some institutional costs are also difficult to calculate. A narrow focus on ticket income can squeeze intellectual substance out of an exhibition. If content is weakened, the exhibition may fail both educationally and financially. A museum therefore needs to balance major events with regular exhibitions. This approach is easier where there is enough gallery space and alternative funding for less heavily promoted fare. The best course is to study what the local community wants. At the same time, museums must ensure that their everyday programme remains enduring.

parts.name: Passage 2
parts.passageHtml:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14-26, which are based on Reading Passage 2 below.

Coastal Archaeology of Britain

A. The recognition of the wealth and diversity of England’s coastal archaeology has been one of the most important developments of recent decades. Some elements of this enormous resource have long been known. The so-called ‘submerged forests’ off the coasts of England, sometimes containing clear evidence of human activity, had attracted the attention of antiquarians since at least the 1740s. However, serious and systematic investigation of the archaeological potential of the coast began only in the early 1980s, transforming what had once been a specialist interest into a significant area of research.

B. It is possible to trace a variety of causes for this concentration of effort and interest. During the 1980s and 1990s, scientific research into climate change and its environmental impact spilled into a much broader public debate as awareness of these issues increased. In particular, reports published in 1983 and 1992 drew attention to the prospect of rising sea levels and their consequences for coastal environments. At the same time, archaeologists became increasingly concerned that the destruction caused by natural processes of coastal erosion, together with human activity, was having a growing impact on archaeological remains. Between 1985 and 1995, the number of coastal surveys undertaken in England more than doubled.

C. The dominant process affecting the physical form of England during the post-glacial period was the rise in the altitude of sea level relative to the land as glaciers melted and the landmass readjusted. In some regions, relative sea level increased by approximately 35 metres. The encroachment of the sea led to the loss of vast areas of land now beneath the North Sea and the English Channel, including the disappearance of the land bridge that once connected Britain and France. These developments must have been immensely significant for prehistoric populations. Yet despite the fact that sea-level change is comparatively well documented, its effects on human communities have received surprisingly limited attention from archaeologists.

D. So great has been the rise in sea level and the consequent regression of the coast that much of the archaeological evidence now exposed in coastal areas, whether being eroded or revealed as buried land surfaces, is derived from what was originally terrestrial occupation. Its present location is therefore often the result of later processes unrelated to the activities that created it. Nevertheless, coastal environments frequently provide excellent conditions for preservation. Important examples include the Neolithic structure excavated at the Stumble in Essex, where organic materials survived in remarkably good condition.

E. In some locations, these buried land surfaces do contain evidence for human exploitation of coastal environments, and similar discoveries have been made elsewhere around the modern shoreline. However, our understanding remains limited. We are not yet in a position to make even preliminary estimates regarding such fundamental issues as the overall importance of the coast in past societies, the extent to which people depended upon marine resources, or whether coastal settlements differed significantly from those located inland.

F. The most striking evidence for the use of the sea is found in boats. Most known wrecks around Britain are of post-medieval date and offer an unparalleled opportunity for research. Earlier vessels are far rarer. The prehistoric sewn-plank boats discovered in locations such as Dover and the Humber estuary belong largely to the period between 1800 BC and 1000 BC. After this, there is a gap in the archaeological record of roughly one thousand years before boats reappeared using a very different technology. Boatbuilding must have been a major activity along much of the coast. These vessels were among the most sophisticated artefacts created by premodern societies, and further research into their production and use has the potential to improve our understanding of technological development.

G. Boats required places to land, yet our knowledge of these facilities remains very patchy. In many cases, natural beaches and shorelines would have sufficed, leaving little archaeological evidence behind. In later periods, however, ports, harbours, quays, wharves, and jetties became increasingly common. While some attention has been given to the waterfront archaeology of important Roman and medieval towns, the multitude of smaller landing places has received far less study. Unfortunately, modern redevelopment and other forms of coastal change are subjecting many of these sites to unprecedented pressure, and only a limited number of surveys have been undertaken.

H. One of the most important revelations of recent research has been the scale of industrial activity along the coast. More than 60 percent of documented coastal industries are connected with fishing or salt production. Although many methods of fishing leave little archaeological trace, surveys have revealed extensive facilities for procuring fish and shellfish. Particularly impressive are the elaborate wooden fish weirs found in areas such as Essex and the Severn Estuary. Some extend for more than 300 metres and are highly responsive to aerial photography in shallow water. Salt production was also significant, with some coastal sites capable of producing several hundred tonnes annually. Other industries exploited resources that outcropped near the coast, taking advantage of convenient transport links. Despite their importance, many of these activities remain poorly documented.

I. Some appreciation of the variety and significance of archaeological remains preserved within the coastal zone, albeit still incomplete, can be gained from recent research. At the same time, the difficulty of protecting this resource is becoming increasingly apparent. Human threats include urban expansion, the redevelopment of historic waterfronts, and the growing provision of tourist facilities such as marinas. Natural pressures remain equally serious. The most significant concern is the continuing rise in sea level, which is currently predicted to average between 3 and 4 millimetres per year in some parts of England. More than 1,000 coastal archaeological sites are considered vulnerable to future damage. The complex web of organisations responsible for managing the coastline means that responding effectively to these threats will continue to pose a major challenge for archaeologists.

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14-26, which are based on Reading Passage 2 below.

Coastal Archaeology of Britain

A. The recognition of the wealth and diversity of England’s coastal archaeology has been one of the most important developments of recent decades. Some elements of this enormous resource have long been known. The so-called ‘submerged forests’ off the coasts of England, sometimes containing clear evidence of human activity, had attracted the attention of antiquarians since at least the 1740s. However, serious and systematic investigation of the archaeological potential of the coast began only in the early 1980s, transforming what had once been a specialist interest into a significant area of research.

B. It is possible to trace a variety of causes for this concentration of effort and interest. During the 1980s and 1990s, scientific research into climate change and its environmental impact spilled into a much broader public debate as awareness of these issues increased. In particular, reports published in 1983 and 1992 drew attention to the prospect of rising sea levels and their consequences for coastal environments. At the same time, archaeologists became increasingly concerned that the destruction caused by natural processes of coastal erosion, together with human activity, was having a growing impact on archaeological remains. Between 1985 and 1995, the number of coastal surveys undertaken in England more than doubled.

C. The dominant process affecting the physical form of England during the post-glacial period was the rise in the altitude of sea level relative to the land as glaciers melted and the landmass readjusted. In some regions, relative sea level increased by approximately 35 metres. The encroachment of the sea led to the loss of vast areas of land now beneath the North Sea and the English Channel, including the disappearance of the land bridge that once connected Britain and France. These developments must have been immensely significant for prehistoric populations. Yet despite the fact that sea-level change is comparatively well documented, its effects on human communities have received surprisingly limited attention from archaeologists.

D. So great has been the rise in sea level and the consequent regression of the coast that much of the archaeological evidence now exposed in coastal areas, whether being eroded or revealed as buried land surfaces, is derived from what was originally terrestrial occupation. Its present location is therefore often the result of later processes unrelated to the activities that created it. Nevertheless, coastal environments frequently provide excellent conditions for preservation. Important examples include the Neolithic structure excavated at the Stumble in Essex, where organic materials survived in remarkably good condition.

E. In some locations, these buried land surfaces do contain evidence for human exploitation of coastal environments, and similar discoveries have been made elsewhere around the modern shoreline. However, our understanding remains limited. We are not yet in a position to make even preliminary estimates regarding such fundamental issues as the overall importance of the coast in past societies, the extent to which people depended upon marine resources, or whether coastal settlements differed significantly from those located inland.

F. The most striking evidence for the use of the sea is found in boats. Most known wrecks around Britain are of post-medieval date and offer an unparalleled opportunity for research. Earlier vessels are far rarer. The prehistoric sewn-plank boats discovered in locations such as Dover and the Humber estuary belong largely to the period between 1800 BC and 1000 BC. After this, there is a gap in the archaeological record of roughly one thousand years before boats reappeared using a very different technology. Boatbuilding must have been a major activity along much of the coast. These vessels were among the most sophisticated artefacts created by premodern societies, and further research into their production and use has the potential to improve our understanding of technological development.

G. Boats required places to land, yet our knowledge of these facilities remains very patchy. In many cases, natural beaches and shorelines would have sufficed, leaving little archaeological evidence behind. In later periods, however, ports, harbours, quays, wharves, and jetties became increasingly common. While some attention has been given to the waterfront archaeology of important Roman and medieval towns, the multitude of smaller landing places has received far less study. Unfortunately, modern redevelopment and other forms of coastal change are subjecting many of these sites to unprecedented pressure, and only a limited number of surveys have been undertaken.

H. One of the most important revelations of recent research has been the scale of industrial activity along the coast. More than 60 percent of documented coastal industries are connected with fishing or salt production. Although many methods of fishing leave little archaeological trace, surveys have revealed extensive facilities for procuring fish and shellfish. Particularly impressive are the elaborate wooden fish weirs found in areas such as Essex and the Severn Estuary. Some extend for more than 300 metres and are highly responsive to aerial photography in shallow water. Salt production was also significant, with some coastal sites capable of producing several hundred tonnes annually. Other industries exploited resources that outcropped near the coast, taking advantage of convenient transport links. Despite their importance, many of these activities remain poorly documented.

I. Some appreciation of the variety and significance of archaeological remains preserved within the coastal zone, albeit still incomplete, can be gained from recent research. At the same time, the difficulty of protecting this resource is becoming increasingly apparent. Human threats include urban expansion, the redevelopment of historic waterfronts, and the growing provision of tourist facilities such as marinas. Natural pressures remain equally serious. The most significant concern is the continuing rise in sea level, which is currently predicted to average between 3 and 4 millimetres per year in some parts of England. More than 1,000 coastal archaeological sites are considered vulnerable to future damage. The complex web of organisations responsible for managing the coastline means that responding effectively to these threats will continue to pose a major challenge for archaeologists.

parts.passageHtml:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27-40, which are based on Reading Passage 3.

Does class size matter?

A. Of all the reforms advanced as remedies for educational underperformance, few possess the uncomplicated public appeal of placing fewer children with each teacher, because the proposal appears to promise individual attention without requiring families to understand complex theories of learning. During the past generation, class-size reduction has therefore moved beyond a specialised academic debate and become a highly visible political intervention, with many education authorities adopting policies intended to limit pupil numbers in the early years. Yet its intuitive attractiveness should not be mistaken for proof that it is the decisive influence on educational success, since teachers, curricula, family circumstances and school resources also shape what children achieve.

B. Some investigators have examined administrative records and identified a broad decline in pupil–teacher ratios over time, while national assessment outcomes have not improved in a similarly straightforward manner; however, this trend does not necessarily demonstrate that smaller classes make no difference, because such figures combine pupils educated under markedly different circumstances. Schools strive not merely to raise test performance but also to reduce dropout rates, support pupils with learning difficulties and retain young people who might otherwise leave education early, any of which can alter average results independently of class size. In addition, a cohort containing more pupils from financially well-off households, whose parents have high educational attainment and can support learning in the language of instruction, cannot be reliably compared with one facing greater socioeconomic disadvantage. Similar problems arise when teachers differ in experience or mastery of their subjects, or when some schools are more generously outfitted with libraries, technology and specialist support. For this reason, observational comparisons may confound the effect of smaller classes with many other influences, making strong causal conclusions from existing records methodologically unsafe.

C. Among the many studies conducted over several decades, the notable exception in design quality was the STAR project, a controlled study in which children beginning school were allocated by chance either to small classes or to regular classes and then remained in the assigned category until the end of their third year. Teachers were also allocated randomly so that instructional quality would not systematically differ between the two conditions, a safeguard intended to make any subsequent contrast in pupil outcomes a fairer test of class size rather than of staffing advantage. Because the project deployed neither specialised curricular materials nor extensive preparation for small-class teachers, it examined the class-size intervention without simultaneously introducing an entirely different teaching model. Although no field study can eliminate every complication, this methodological structure provided considerably more robust evidence than retrospective records and made STAR central to subsequent debate about educational policy.

D. Reviews of STAR identified an array of benefits for pupils in smaller classrooms, with improvements appearing slightly stronger among Black and Hispanic children, an outcome with particular significance from a policy standpoint because achievement gaps frequently reflect wider demographic and economic disadvantage. Nevertheless, the evidence cannot establish that these gains persist for many years after children return to ordinary classrooms, so it would be unsafe to extrapolate an immediate advantage into a permanent educational transformation. A further complication was that too many pupils moved from regular classes into smaller ones during the project, apparently because school personnel caved in to pressure from parents, thereby weakening the separation between the comparison groups. This breach of implementation fidelity complicates interpretation, but it does not undermine the statistically significant conclusion that pupils placed in smaller classes obtained a measurable short-term benefit.

E. The large-scale California programme stands less as a model worthy of emulation than as evidence that promising research can be poorly translated into statewide practice, because it imposed class-size reduction across both prosperous and disadvantaged districts despite a serious shortage of suitably qualified teachers, especially in poorer communities. Such a uniform approach may have been politically expedient, since it offered the same headline reform everywhere, but it ignored the heterogeneous capacities of schools to recruit effective staff and consequently exacerbated the disparity between rich and poor districts. Better-paying, more affluent communities were able to attract stronger teachers, including some who had previously worked in schools serving children with greater needs, so a reform intended to promote opportunity partly redistributed existing expertise away from its most vulnerable pupils. California recorded only modest achievement benefits, whereas the smaller SAGE programme was noteworthy because it concentrated support on schools serving substantial numbers of low-income children rather than assuming every district faced the same problem. This deliberate stratification did not, by itself, settle every question about cost or long-term outcomes, but it offered a more targeted basis for examining whether reduced classes might assist disadvantaged communities.

F. Taken together, STAR and SAGE make it difficult to maintain that smaller classes never assist learning, while California demonstrates that the same strategy, introduced with insufficient forethought about teacher supply and local conditions, can absorb enormous public expenditure while producing only minuscule gains and even worsening inequalities in the short term. The broader lesson is not that governments should abandon class-size reduction, nor that they should make it the dominant educational priority, but that effectiveness depends on where the reform is directed, how faithfully it is implemented and what resources accompany it. Legislators and administrators therefore require reliable comparisons between this approach and alternatives such as teacher development, early intervention or additional support for disadvantaged schools before they can reach sensible policy decisions. A popular reform becomes a defensible policy only when its anticipated benefits, financial cost and potential for unintended harm have been evaluated together.
